vendors.detected: aws-amplify v6.6.0 (Amazon Cognito, modular v6 API)

comprehensive.reason: Amplify configuration entry point — the load-bearing file for the storage seam.
Candidate boundary module: needed to distinguish real anti-corruption layer from leaky facade.
Auth-consuming integration point: where refresh, token-type, and injected-vs-imported all surface.
App-layer component: confirmed vendor-type leak, inline claim reads, and hard-coded roles.
Second app-layer component: needed to establish the spread of inline claim reads across files.
Page-level code: vendor-specific fetchUserAttributes and custom-attribute surface.
The only auth test: needed to classify it as vendor-shape mocking vs boundary contract suite.

findings.statement: UserBadge.tsx imports fetchAuthSession and the vendor's AuthSession type directly from aws-amplify/auth into app-layer UI code.
The vendor's AuthSession is used as a React state type in an app-layer component — the vendor shape crosses the boundary directly into UI code.
An app-layer exported function returns Promise<AuthSession>, so every caller of it is now typed against the vendor's session shape.
AdminPanel.tsx imports fetchAuthSession directly from aws-amplify/auth — a second component wired straight to the vendor, evidencing the spread.
The axios API client imports fetchAuthSession directly and is hard-wired to Amplify at the module level rather than receiving an injected auth port.
Profile.tsx imports fetchUserAttributes and the vendor's FetchUserAttributesOutput type directly into a page — both a direct-import leak (B2) and a vendor-type leak (B1).

src/lib/auth-helpers.ts looks like a boundary but is a leaky facade: it re-exports vendor functions and returns the vendor's AuthSession and AuthUser unchanged, so the vendor's shape still crosses to every caller.

evidence.quote: import { fetchAuthSession, getCurrentUser, signOut, AuthSession, AuthUser } from 'aws-amplify/auth';

findings.note: This is the exact 'looks bounded, isn't' trap the methodology warns about — the shape passes straight through the wrapper.

findings.statement: No AuthPort / AuthAdapter-style interface exists anywhere; no call site receives auth as an injected capability.
checked_patterns: AuthPort / AuthAdapter / IAuthProvider interface or type declaration
port-shaped interface with getAuthHeaders / getPrincipal / onRefresh methods
any parameter of a domain type wrapping vendor auth

findings.statement: The only auth test mocks aws-amplify/auth and asserts against the vendor's idToken.payload['cognito:groups'] shape — the classic vendor-shape mock that passes today and dies on migration.
No conformance/contract suite tests the auth boundary itself; the only auth test mocks the vendor SDK.
checked_patterns: tests asserting against a domain Principal / Session / AuthPort shape
any auth test file NOT mocking aws-amplify/auth
boundary/adapter tests in src/lib/ or a dedicated contracts/ directory

findings.statement: No SSR/server auth surface exists in this app — no aws-amplify/auth/server imports, no createServerRunner, no client/server branching in auth-adjacent code. Client-only, so the client/server-split concern does not arise.
checked_patterns: typeof window !== 'undefined' branching around auth acquisition

findings.statement: Amplify v6 is initialized with no storage customization at all — no v6 setKeyValueStorage call, no custom tokenProvider, no built-in selector, and (checked for a mid-migration mix) no legacy v5 storage: or cookieStorage: config either. Tokens are stored in the vendor default localStorage under the CognitoIdentityServiceProvider.* prefix.
checked_patterns: custom tokenProvider passed to Amplify.configure — v6 deep customization
built-in selectors passed to setKeyValueStorage (defaultStorage / sessionStorage / new CookieStorage() from aws-amplify/utils) — look-alike, not custom
v5 storage: class inside Amplify.configure({ Auth: { ... } }) — legacy custom adapter
v5 cookieStorage: config object inside Amplify.configure({ Auth: { ... } }) — legacy look-alike selector
findings.note: Version-qualified: Amplify v6 (from package.json aws-amplify ^6.6.0). Even if a custom KeyValueStorage were added, note the profile's caveat — it overrides only the TokenStore; identityId (if Identity Pools were in use) would still live in localStorage. Identity Pools are not configured here.

findings.statement: The axios request interceptor calls fetchAuthSession() on every request with no single-flight dedup, no forceRefresh path, and no failure branch — inherited vendor refresh magic, load-bearing on browser-readable tokens.
No single-flight dedup around refresh: N concurrent 401s (or N concurrent request interceptors racing on an expiring session) would each drive their own fetchAuthSession call.
checked_patterns: any Promise-caching / memoization wrapper around fetchAuthSession or forceRefresh

findings.statement: No explicit onSessionExpired / 401-response handler exists: nothing catches a refresh failure and routes to sign-out or login. The failure path is whatever Amplify does silently.
checked_patterns: axios `interceptors.response` for 401 handling with retry + failure route

findings.statement: No Amplify Hub listener for auth lifecycle events — no sign-out propagation, no multi-tab session sync, no reaction to tokenRefresh_failure.
checked_patterns: cross-tab BroadcastChannel / storage-event handler for auth state
any subscriber to tokenRefresh / tokenRefresh_failure / signedOut events

findings.statement: UserBadge reads the Cognito-namespaced 'cognito:groups' claim inline from the vendor's idToken payload — vendor-specific claim shape in app-layer code.
UserBadge reads the Cognito-namespaced 'cognito:username' claim inline from the vendor's idToken payload.
AdminPanel reads 'cognito:groups' inline from a second component — the coupling is spread, not one accident.
Profile page reads a Cognito custom attribute inline via a hard-coded 'custom:tenantId' key — provider-specific attribute surface in page-level code.
The vendor-specific fetchUserAttributes API is invoked from page-level code rather than localized behind an adapter.
UserBadge encodes the authorization decision as a hard-coded 'admin' role string checked against a Cognito group.
AdminPanel encodes multiple hard-coded role strings ('admin', 'billing-admin') for its authorization decision.
The outbound API Authorization header is the Cognito ID token, not the access token — authentication and authorization are coupled to the same token, and the access token is never read.
No domain Principal type, no policy layer, and no centralized permission check — every authorization decision is an inline claim read at a call site.
checked_patterns: any RBAC/ABAC helper that consumes a Principal, not raw claims

b1_anti_corruption.note: AuthSession, AuthUser, and FetchUserAttributesOutput cross into app-layer signatures and React state. The 'wrapper' in src/lib/auth-helpers.ts is a leaky facade — it re-exports vendor functions unchanged.

b2_injected.note: aws-amplify/auth is imported at the module level in five app-layer files; no AuthPort interface exists and nothing is injected.

b3_contract_tested.note: The only auth test mocks the vendor SDK and asserts against its idToken.payload shape — the exact anti-pattern a contract suite would replace.

b4_client_server_split.note: This is a client-only React SPA — no SSR surface, no aws-amplify/auth/server usage, no client/server branching. The concern does not arise here; a status of 'absent' would be a false gap.

cognito.note: Amplify v6 with no storage customization at all — tokens live in browser localStorage under CognitoIdentityServiceProvider.*. This is the load-bearing dependency the maintainer's planned HttpOnly-cookie move will collide with.

storage.recommended_seam: A domain AuthPort (Session, Principal, getAuthHeaders, refresh, onSessionExpired) with a custom KeyValueStorageInterface adapter plugged into cognitoUserPoolsTokenProvider.setKeyValueStorage. The adapter lives inside the port; app code speaks your Session type only. For HttpOnly cookies specifically, tokens must be written server-side, so the storage adapter becomes a shim that calls a same-origin server route — the seam is the same, the adapter is what changes per storage strategy.

cost_evidence.basis: The storage seam itself lives in one file (src/lib/amplify-config.ts) and setKeyValueStorage is a one-call change. The multiplier is downstream: refresh is inherited via a bare fetchAuthSession() in the API interceptor, and Amplify's silent refresh requires JS-readable tokens — HttpOnly cookies invalidate it. So a storage adapter alone will silently break refresh; the real cost is 'storage adapter + owned refresh + probably a server route,' not one config edit.

cognito.note: Fully inherited: bare fetchAuthSession() in the interceptor, no single-flight dedup, no failure path, no Hub listener for lifecycle events. The vendor's silent refresh is doing all the work — and only works while tokens are JS-readable.

refresh.recommended_seam: An owned 401 response interceptor with single-flight dedup (one refresh promise for N concurrent 401s), fetchAuthSession({ forceRefresh: true }) inside it, and an explicit onSessionExpired failure path. Because HttpOnly-cookie tokens cannot be read or refreshed by browser JS, the refresh path will need a server route (e.g. POST /auth/refresh) that the client hits — the seam is the same, the adapter changes.

cost_evidence.basis: Only one call site (src/api/client.ts) attaches auth to outbound requests, so the interceptor rewrite is contained. But nothing exists to extend: single-flight, failure path, and lifecycle events all have to be built from scratch, and post-storage-move the refresh has to go through a server route. Contained blast radius, non-trivial net-new machinery.

cognito.note: Provider-specific surface (cognito: namespaced claims, custom:* attributes, fetchUserAttributes) reaches into two components and one page. There is no adapter to hide any of it.

identity_provider.recommended_seam: Localize every cognito:* claim read, every custom:* attribute read, and every fetchUserAttributes call to a single Cognito adapter behind the AuthPort. App code sees a domain Principal (id, displayName, tenantId, roles, permissions) — never vendor claim shapes.

cost_evidence.basis: Coupling is spread across three app-layer files (UserBadge, AdminPanel, Profile) with four distinct vendor surfaces used inline (cognito:groups, cognito:username, custom:tenantId, fetchUserAttributes/FetchUserAttributesOutput). No adapter exists, no Principal exists — a provider swap here means both introducing the boundary AND rewriting every one of those reads. Absolute effort would be non-trivial.

cognito.note: Authorization decisions are inline reads of cognito:groups with hard-coded role strings in two components, and outbound API auth uses the ID token — the access token is never read. RBAC/ABAC has no place to land: no Principal, no policy layer, and the token that would carry richer permissions isn't the one the backend gets.

authorization.recommended_seam: The AuthPort produces a domain Principal (roles, permissions) mapped from Cognito claims inside the adapter. Authorization decisions flow through a single policy function (e.g. can(principal, action)) — no inline claim reads, no hard-coded role strings. Attach the access token (session.tokens.accessToken.toString()) — not the ID token — to outbound API calls; the ID token stays on the identity side.

cost_evidence.basis: Two components read cognito:groups inline with four hard-coded role strings between them (admin, billing-admin); no Principal, no policy layer, no permission vocabulary — every authorization decision is a from-scratch build. The token-type change is a one-line swap in src/api/client.ts, but is meaningless without the backend also accepting the access token, and pointless without a policy layer to consume finer permissions. The three changes are coupled; sequencing matters.

storage.notes: moving token storage to HttpOnly cookies next quarter

authorization.notes: roles are outgrowing the current admin flag

judgment_calls.question: True retrofit cost in your team's terms — the mechanical basis puts storage/refresh at moderate and identity_provider/authorization at high, but the wall-clock cost depends on team bandwidth, test-coverage state, and how the backend is prepared to accept access tokens. Confirm the cost levels above before sequencing.
judgment_calls.context: The audit's cost_evidence is a mechanical read (boundary quality, spread of coupling, confirmed call-site counts). The 'how long will this take in this org' number is yours.

judgment_calls.question: Does your backend today accept the Cognito access token, or is it validating (and reading claims from) the ID token? If the backend is coupled to the ID token, the client-side swap is a two-sided change, not a one-line edit.
judgment_calls.context: src/api/client.ts:17 sends the ID token. Moving to access tokens is client-cheap, but breaks the backend if the backend is verifying ID-token claims or aud values.

judgment_calls.question: For the HttpOnly-cookie move: is there a same-origin server route you can attach to (e.g. Next.js API route, existing gateway), or will infra need to grow one? The storage adapter itself is small; the cookie-setting endpoint isn't.
judgment_calls.context: HttpOnly cookies can't be written by browser JS, so the storage seam becomes a client shim over a server route. That's an infra decision, not an app-layer one.

backlog.task: Introduce a domain AuthPort and move the boundary behind it (starting with src/lib/auth-helpers.ts, which today is a leaky facade).
backlog.why: Every planned change (storage, refresh, authorization) needs a seam that doesn't exist. Cost evidence: absent boundary across all four B-signals; five app-layer direct imports plus a leaky facade. Without this step the other three tasks each have to introduce their own boundary and undo the vendor-type leaks in every touched file. This is the multiplier — do it first or pay it four times.

backlog.task: Introduce a domain Principal + single policy layer; remove inline cognito:groups reads and hard-coded role strings from UserBadge and AdminPanel.
backlog.why: Maintainer's likelihood: HIGH (RBAC/ABAC planned; 'roles are outgrowing the current admin flag'). Cost evidence: high — inline claim reads in two components with four hard-coded role strings, no Principal, no policy function. RBAC has no place to land until this exists. Coupled with task 3: the access-token swap is meaningless without a policy layer to consume richer permissions.

backlog.task: Own refresh: 401 response interceptor with single-flight dedup, forceRefresh, and an onSessionExpired failure path.
backlog.why: Maintainer's likelihood: MEDIUM ('tied to storage'). Cost evidence: moderate — one call site, but everything (single-flight, failure path, lifecycle) has to be built from nothing. Rank order: this MUST land before the storage move ships. Amplify's silent refresh only works while tokens are JS-readable; the moment HttpOnly cookies land, an unowned refresh path breaks silently across every authenticated call.

backlog.task: Write a custom KeyValueStorageInterface adapter and plug it into cognitoUserPoolsTokenProvider.setKeyValueStorage (as the local step of the HttpOnly-cookie move; the cookie side lives on the server).
backlog.why: Maintainer's likelihood: HIGH ('moving to HttpOnly cookies next quarter'; cost_confirmed: MODERATE). Cost evidence: moderate — the seam itself is one file, but it must ship together with the owned refresh path (task 3) and a same-origin server route for cookie-setting. Sequence AFTER refresh is owned; otherwise inherited refresh breaks the same day the cookies land.

backlog.task: Swap the API Authorization header from the ID token to the access token; coordinate with the backend to accept it.
backlog.why: One-line change on the client (src/api/client.ts:15,17) — but real cost depends on whether the backend today verifies ID-token claims or aud. Rank behind the Principal/policy work: sending an access token is only meaningful if there is a policy layer consuming the permissions it carries. Do these together, or the swap is symbolic.

backlog.task: Replace the vendor-mock auth test with a contract/conformance suite that runs against the AuthPort.
backlog.why: Cost evidence: low once the port from task 1 exists — the current test (__tests__/auth.test.ts) is the wrong shape and can be rewritten. Ranked last because it depends on task 1, but omitting it leaves the boundary structurally present and untestable — the storage/refresh/RBAC changes ship 'and pray' instead of 'make the contract green.'

synthesis.posture: Heavily calcified — no real boundary; all four axes leak into app code.

headline.text: Two of the changes you already have on the roadmap collide with what the code is doing today. The planned HttpOnly-cookie move (next quarter) will silently break refresh: src/api/client.ts calls a bare fetchAuthSession() every request and Amplify's silent refresh only works while tokens are JS-readable — so own refresh before storage moves. And the planned RBAC change has no place to land: authorization is inline cognito:groups reads with hard-coded role strings in src/components/UserBadge.tsx and src/components/AdminPanel.tsx, and outbound API auth uses the ID token — the access token that would carry finer permissions is never read.
